source_text: Videamus nunc, an et cetera domini edicta congruant perpetuo fugae praecepto. Primo quidem, si a deo persecutio est, quale est, ut idem fugiendam eam mandet, qui et infert? Quam si evadi vellet, melius non immitteret, ne voluntatem suam alia voluntate praevaricari videretur. Aut pati enim nos voluit persecutionem aut fugere. Si fugere, quomodo pati? si pati, quomodo fugere? Iam vero quanta inaequalitas sententiarum iubentis fugere et invitantis ad passionem contrariam fugae. Qui confessus fuerit me et ego confitebor illum coram patre meo. Quomodo confitebitur fugiens? quomodo fugiet confitens? Qui mei confusus fuerit, et ego confundar eius coram patre. Si devito passionem, confundor confessionem. Felices qui persecutionem passi fuerint causa nominis mei. Infelices ergo qui fugiendo ex praecepto non erunt passi. Qui sustinuerit in finem, iste salvabitur. Quid ergo me iubens fugere vis in finem sustinere? Tanta diversitas sententiarum si non congruit divinae gravitati, apparet ex his quoque praeceptum fugae suam tunc habuisse rationem, quam ostendimus. Sed infirmitatem, inquit, quorundam prospiciens dominus pro sua humanitate nihilominus et portum fugae demonstravit. Non enim idoneus erat etiam sine fuga tam turpi et indigno et servili praesidio salvos facere in persecutione quos sciret infirmos. Atquin non fovet, sed recusat semper infirmos, primum docens non fugiendos esse persecutors, sed potius non timendos. Nolite timere eos qui corpus occidere possunt, animae autem nihil valent facere, sed timete eum qui et corpus et animam perdere potest in gehennam. Atque exinde quae timidis praefinit? Qui pluris fecerit animam suam quam me, non est me dignus, et qui non tollit crucem suam et sequitur me, non potest esse meus discipulus. Postremo in Apocalypsi non fugam timidis offert, sed inter ceteros reprobos particulam in stagnum sulphuris et ignis, quod est mors secunda.
thought_title: The Lord's commands contradict a perpetual command to flee
orientation: Tertullian is arguing that the Lord's own sayings about confession, suffering, and endurance are incompatible with a lasting command to flee persecution.
pass_a_gloss: Let us see now whether also the other edicts of the Lord agree with a perpetual command of flight. First indeed, if persecution is from God, what sort of thing is it, that the same one commands that it be fled, who also brings it? If he wished it to be avoided, he would better not send it, lest he seem to have his own will violated by another will. For either he wanted us to suffer persecution or to flee. If to flee, how to suffer? if to suffer, how to flee? Now truly how great an inconsistency of the opinions of one commanding flight and inviting to a passion contrary to flight. He who has confessed me, I also will confess him before my father. How will he confess while fleeing? how will he flee while confessing? He who has been ashamed of me, I also will be ashamed of him before my father. If I avoid passion, I am ashamed of confession. Happy are those who will have suffered persecution for the sake of my name. Unhappy therefore are those who by fleeing according to the command will not have suffered. He who has endured to the end, that one will be saved. Why then, commanding me to flee, do you want me to endure to the end? So great a diversity of opinions if it does not agree with divine seriousness, it appears from these things also that the command of flight had its own reason at that time, which we have shown. But looking out for the weakness, he says, of certain ones, the Lord in accordance with his humanity nevertheless also showed a harbor of flight. For he was not able also without flight, so base and unworthy and slavish a protection, to save in persecution those whom he knew to be weak. But on the contrary he does not cherish, but always rejects the weak, first teaching that persecutors are not to be fled, but rather not to be feared. Do not fear those who can kill the body, but can do nothing to the soul, but fear him who can destroy both body and soul in hell. And then what does he prescribe for the cowardly? He who has valued his own soul more than me, is not worthy of me, and he who does not take up his cross and follow me, cannot be my disciple. Finally in Revelation he does not offer flight to the cowardly, but among the other rejected ones a share in the lake of sulphur and fire, which is the second death.

choices.why: The verb means to transgress or act contrary to; here God's will would be contradicted by another will if he both sent persecution and commanded flight.
Tertullian is pointing out the logical contradiction between commanding flight and inviting to passion; 'inconsistency' captures the unevenness or lack of uniformity.
The passive of confundo means to be confounded or ashamed; this matches the Gospel saying about being ashamed of Christ.
The metaphor is of a safe harbor or refuge; Tertullian is quoting the objector's claim that the Lord showed a place of safety in flight.
Praesidium means defense or protection; here it is qualified as base, unworthy, and slavish, emphasizing the shamefulness of flight as a means of safety.
Particula is a diminutive of pars, meaning a small part or portion; in Revelation the cowardly receive their portion in the lake of fire.

pass_b_english: Let us now see whether the rest of the Lord's commands agree with a perpetual command to flee. First of all, if persecution comes from God, what sense does it make for the same God who sends it to command that it be fled? If he wanted it to be avoided, he would do better not to send it at all, so that his will would not seem to be violated by another will. For either he wanted us to suffer persecution or to flee. If to flee, how can we suffer? If to suffer, how can we flee? And what a great inconsistency there is between the opinions of one who commands flight and one who invites us to a suffering that is the opposite of flight.

"Whoever confesses me, I will also confess before my Father" (Matthew 10:32). How will he confess while fleeing? How will he flee while confessing? "Whoever has been ashamed of me, I will also be ashamed of him before my Father" (Matthew 10:33). If I avoid suffering, I am ashamed of confession. "Blessed are those who suffer persecution for the sake of my name" (Matthew 5:11). Unblessed, then, are those who by fleeing according to the command will not have suffered. "Whoever endures to the end will be saved" (Matthew 10:22). So why do you command me to flee, yet want me to endure to the end? If such a great diversity of opinions does not agree with divine seriousness, it is clear from these sayings too that the command to flee had its own reason at that time, which we have shown.

But, someone says, the Lord, looking out for the weakness of certain people in his humanity, nevertheless also pointed out a harbor of flight. For he was not able, without flight—such a base, unworthy, and slavish protection—to save in persecution those he knew to be weak.

But he does not cherish the weak; he always rejects them. First he teaches that persecutors are not to be fled, but rather not to be feared. "Do not fear those who can kill the body but can do nothing to the soul; rather fear him who can destroy both body and soul in hell" (Matthew 10:28). And then what does he prescribe for the cowardly? "Whoever values his own life more than me is not worthy of me, and whoever does not take up his cross and follow me cannot be my disciple" (Matthew 10:37-38; Luke 14:27). Finally, in Revelation he does not offer flight to the cowardly, but among the rest of the rejected ones a share in the lake that burns with fire and brimstone, which is the second death (Revelation 21:8).

last_rejected.why: 'confundor' is passive: 'I am put to shame,' not 'I am ashamed of.' Agency reversed.
last_rejected.fix: If I avoid suffering, I am put to shame in my confession.
last_rejected.ruling: confundor passive can mean 'I am ashamed', matching translation

last_rejected.quote: Unblessed, then, are those who by fleeing according to the command will not have suffered.
last_rejected.source_quote: Infelices ergo qui fugiendo ex praecepto non erunt passi.
last_rejected.why: 'Infelices' means 'unfortunate/wretched,' not 'unblessed,' which reverses the contrast with 'Blessed.'
last_rejected.fix: Unfortunate, then, are those who by fleeing according to the command will not have suffered.

last_rejected.quote: First he teaches that persecutors are not to be fled, but rather not to be feared.

last_rejected.quote: But, someone says, the Lord, looking out for the weakness of certain people in his humanity, nevertheless also pointed out a harbor of flight.
last_rejected.source_quote: Sed infirmitatem, inquit, quorundam prospiciens dominus pro sua humanitate nihilominus et portum fugae demonstravit.
last_rejected.why: The English misattributes the speaker; the Lord is speaking, not an unnamed person.

polish.changed: Split the objector's argument into its own paragraph so the reader can clearly see where the objection ends and Tertullian's reply begins, and clarified the flow of the scriptural argument.

notes.quote: But, someone says, the Lord, looking out for the weakness of certain people
notes.why: The objector's argument runs for several sentences without clear closing; reader may lose track of where the objection ends and Tertullian's reply begins.
notes.fix: Use quotation marks or a clear break to mark where the objector's words end.
